familyNishadha.name: Nishadha
familyNishadha.note: Nala's janapada, distinct from the Nishada forest tribe of Ekalavya

people.notes: Chandra Deva (also Soma), the radiant deva of the moon and of the soma nectar; progenitor and eponym of the Chandravamsha, the lunar dynasty from which both the Kurus and the Yadavas descend.
Budha Deva, the deva of the planet Mercury and son of Chandra; husband of Ila.
Son of Budha and Ila; first emperor of the lunar line, famed for his love of the apsara Urvashi.
Son of Pururavas and Urvashi.
Son of Ayus; so mighty he briefly took Indra's throne, then fell for his pride and became a serpent.
Son of Nahusha; a great emperor cursed with old age, which his youngest son Puru bore for him. His five sons founded five peoples.
Child of Vaivasvata Manu. Lived alternately as the woman Ila (mother of Pururavas by Budha) and the man Sudyumna, whose reign gave the sons below.
The apsara beloved of Pururavas and mother of Ayus.
First wife of Yayati; daughter of Shukracharya, preceptor of the asuras. Mother of Yadu and Turvasu.
Second wife of Yayati; daughter of the asura king Vrishaparva. Mother of Druhyu, Anu and Puru.
Eldest son of Yayati and Devayani; progenitor of the Yadavas (the Yadu line), into which Krishna is born.
Son of Yayati and Devayani; ancestor of the Yavana peoples.
Son of Yayati and Sharmishtha; ancestor of the Bhoja peoples.
Son of Yayati and Sharmishtha; ancestor of the Mleccha peoples.
Youngest son of Yayati and Sharmishtha; he gave his own youth to his aged father and so inherited the throne, founding the Paurava (Kuru) line.
A Paurava emperor descended from Puru through several generations; husband of Shakuntala and father of Bharata.
Daughter of the sage Vishvamitra and the apsara Menaka, raised by the sage Kanva; wife of Dushyanta and mother of Bharata.
The great emperor son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala, after whom the land Bharatavarsha and the Bharata clan are named.
Son of Brihatkshatra; he built Hastinapura, which carries his name. SB 9.21.21
King some generations after Hastin; eponymous ancestor of the Kurus and of the field of Kurukshetra.
Son of Yadu; the Yadava kings descend from him.
A Yadava king, son of Kroshtu.
A Yadava king of the early Yadu line.
A Yadava king of the early Yadu line.
A Yadava king; progenitor of the Madhava branch, whence Krishna's epithet Madhava. Several generations separate him from Vrishni.
Son of Satvata, and the Vrishni for whom the clan of Krishna is named. SB 9.24.6-12
King of the Kuru line; husband of Sunanda.
Wife of Pratipa; a princess of Shibi and mother of Devapi, Bahlika and Shantanu.
Eldest son of Pratipa; a skin ailment led him to renounce the throne and take to the forest as an ascetic.
Son of Pratipa; ruled the Bahlika kingdom. His descendants fought on the Kaurava side.
Youngest son of Pratipa; became king when Devapi renounced. Father of Bhishma.
Son of Bahlika.
Son of Somadatta; a mighty Kaurava warrior slain by Satyaki at Kurukshetra.
The devi of the sacred river; Shantanu's first wife and mother of Bhishma, whom she bore as the last of the eight Vasus made mortal.

Born Devavrata; took a vow of lifelong celibacy so his father could marry Satyavati, hence 'Bhishma'. He was Prabhasa, the eighth and last of the eight Vasus, cursed to a long mortal life for stealing the sage Vasishtha's cow; his seven brother-Vasus, shown here as Ganga's other sons, she returned at once to heaven. Grandsire and regent of the Kurus; a chiranjivi who chose his own hour of death.
A Vasu, deva of the earth; a brother-Vasu of Bhishma (Prabhasa), borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the pole star; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the moon; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the day and the ethereal space; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the wind; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of fire (Agni); borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the dawn; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A fisherman's daughter, raised by the ferryman Dasharaja; queen of Shantanu and matriarch of the later Kuru line.
A great sage; father of Vyasa by Satyavati before her marriage to Shantanu.

Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa, son of Satyavati and the sage Parashara before her marriage; arranger of the Vedas and composer of the Mahabharat. Biological father, through niyoga, of Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura.
Elder son of Shantanu and Satyavati; a proud king slain young by a gandharva, leaving no heir.
Younger son of Shantanu and Satyavati; wed Ambika and Ambalika but died childless, prompting the niyoga that continued the line.
King of Kashi; his three daughters were carried off from their svayamvara by Bhishma as brides for Vichitravirya.
Eldest Kashi princess; rejected because she loved another, she vowed vengeance on Bhishma and was reborn in Panchala as Shikhandi.
Kashi princess wed to Vichitravirya; mother, through Vyasa's niyoga, of Dhritarashtra, she shut her eyes, so her son was born blind.
Kashi princess wed to Vichitravirya; mother, through Vyasa's niyoga, of Pandu, she paled at the sight of Vyasa, so her son was born pale.
A maidservant of the Kuru queens; mother of Vidura through Vyasa's niyoga.
Born blind to Ambika through Vyasa's niyoga; the elder prince, kept from the throne by his blindness. Father of the Kauravas.
Born pale to Ambalika through Vyasa's niyoga; king of Hastinapura. A curse made his touch fatal to a wife, so his sons were god-begotten.
Born to the maid Parishrami through Vyasa's niyoga; an incarnation of Dharma, wisest counsellor of the Kurus, never king by birth of a servant.
Wife of Vidura.
King of Gandhara; father of Gandhari and Shakuni.
Princess of Gandhara; on marrying the blind Dhritarashtra she bound her own eyes for life. By a boon she bore a hundred sons and a daughter.
Prince of Gandhara, Gandhari's brother; master of the loaded dice, he engineered the Kauravas' schemes against the Pandavas.
Son of Shakuni; the Kauravas' envoy to the Pandava camp.
Eldest of the hundred Kauravas; the crown prince whose enmity for the Pandavas drove the war. At his birth jackals howled, an omen he should be cast out.
Second Kaurava; dragged Draupadi into the assembly and tried to disrobe her, an outrage Bhima avenged by tearing open his breast.
The one Kaurava who spoke up for Draupadi's honour in the dice hall; reckoned the most righteous of the brothers.
One of the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari. Not Nanda of Gokula, who raised Krishna. MBh 1.108
A Kaurava son (not to be confused with the king of Magadha of the same name).
A Kaurava skilled with the mace, often at Duryodhana's side.
The only daughter of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, born after the hundred sons; wed to Jayadratha, king of Sindhu.
Son of Dhritarashtra by the maid Sughada; the one son of that house to cross over and fight on the Pandava side.
A vaishya attendant of the Kuru household; mother of Yuyutsu by Dhritarashtra.
Wife of Duryodhana; a princess of Kalinga.
Daughter of Duryodhana; carried off by Krishna's son Samba, which nearly sparked a war.
Son of Duryodhana (Lakshmana Kumara); slain by Abhimanyu inside the chakravyuha.
King of Sindhu, husband of Dushala; his blocking of the Pandavas at the pass sealed Abhimanyu's death, and Arjuna vowed and took his head the next day.
Son of Jayadratha and Dushala.
Eldest Pandava, begotten of Kunti by Dharma (Yama); the just king, never known to lie.
Second Pandava, begotten of Kunti by Vayu; of superhuman strength, sworn to kill all hundred Kauravas.
Third Pandava, begotten of Kunti by Indra; the supreme archer, friend of Krishna, hearer of the Bhagavad Gita.
Fourth Pandava, twin son of Madri by the Ashvins; matchless horseman and the handsomest of men.
Youngest Pandava, twin son of Madri by the Ashvins; wisest of the brothers and a knower of the future.

Kunti's firstborn, begotten by Surya the sun-god before her marriage; set adrift on the river and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha, so his birth lineage stayed unknown even to him. Half-brother of the Pandavas, he fought and died for Duryodhana, learning his kin too late.
Son of Satkarma, of the Anga line, and a suta by office. Playing on the bank of the Ganga he found a basket with a child in it, and having no son of his own he raised him: Karna. SB 9.23.12-13
Wife of Adhiratha; foster-mother of Karna, whence his name Radheya.
Wife of Karna.
Son of Karna; a warrior slain by Arjuna at Kurukshetra.
Youngest son of Karna and the only one to outlive the war; taken in and cherished by the Pandavas once his parentage was known.
Son of Yudhishthira and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Bhima and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Arjuna and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Nakula and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Sahadeva and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
A rakshasi of the forest who loved Bhima during the Pandavas' exile; mother of Ghatotkacha.
Son of Bhima and Hidimba; a rakshasa prince of great sorcery who grew to manhood in a day and died turning the tide of the war, drawing Karna's infallible weapon onto himself.
Wife of Ghatotkacha; mother of Barbarika.
Son of Ghatotkacha; the archer of the three arrows who vowed to fight for whichever side was losing and so gave up his head to Krishna.
Son of Arjuna and Subhadra; the boy warrior who broke into the chakravyuha and was killed within it, leaving Uttara pregnant with the Kuru line's sole heir.
A Naga princess who wed Arjuna during his wanderings; mother of Iravan and, later, protector of the reborn Arjuna.
Son of Arjuna and Ulupi; raised among the Nagas, he offered himself in sacrifice for the Pandava victory.
Princess of Manipura who wed Arjuna on the condition that their son remain to rule her land; mother of Babhruvahana.
Son of Arjuna and Chitrangada; king of Manipura. Not knowing his father, he met and slew Arjuna in battle during the horse sacrifice; Ulupi's gem restored him to life.
Son of Abhimanyu and Uttara; stillborn but revived by Krishna, he became the sole surviving heir and king of the Kurus after the war.
A princess of Madra; wife of Parikshit and mother of Janamejaya.
Son of Parikshit; the king at whose serpent sacrifice the Mahabharat was first recited by Vaishampayana.
Son of Janamejaya (not to be confused with the Upapandava of the same name); he carried the Kuru throne into the age after the war.
Son of Shatanika; a later Kuru king. The Puranas run the line on through several more kings to Kshemaka, its last.
King of Madra; father of Shalya and Madri.
King of Madra, brother of Madri; a peerless charioteer tricked into fighting for Duryodhana, whom he served as Karna's charioteer.
Princess of Madra; second wife of Pandu and mother, by the Ashvins, of the twins Nakula and Sahadeva. She followed Pandu onto his pyre.
King of Panchala; father of Drupada.
King of Panchala; humiliated by his old classmate Drona, he won from a sacrifice a son to slay Drona and a daughter to wed the Pandavas.
Child of Drupada, the reincarnation of Amba; born a girl and later made a man, whose presence let Bhishma be brought down, for Bhishma would not fight one born a woman.
Son of Drupada, born from the sacrificial fire; commander of the Pandava army, fated to and did slay Drona.
Also Krishnaa and Yajnaseni; born of the sacrificial fire beside Dhrishtadyumna. Won by Arjuna, she became the shared wife of all five Pandavas and empress of Indraprastha.
King of Matsya, in whose court the Pandavas passed their thirteenth year of exile in disguise.
Queen of Virata.
Prince of Matsya (Uttara-kumara / Bhuminjaya); he rode out with the disguised Arjuna against the Kuru cattle-raid.
Princess of Matsya; wed to Abhimanyu and, widowed in the war, mother of Parikshit who carried on the Kuru line.
A Yadava patriarch; father of Devaka and Ugrasena.
Yadava prince, son of Ahuka; father of Devaki.
Yadava king of Mathura, son of Ahuka; deposed by his son Kamsa and restored by Krishna.
Son of Ugrasena; the tyrant of Mathura who jailed Devaki and Vasudeva and was slain by the young Krishna.
Daughter of Devaka, wife of Vasudeva and mother of Krishna; her first sons were killed by her cousin Kamsa.

Shura, son of Vidhuratha of the Vrishni house; ten sons, of whom Vasudeva was the chief, and five daughters, one of them Pritha whom he gave to his friend Kunti. The Bhagavata runs his descent through Chitraratha and Vidhuratha, this tree through Vrishni, and both are recorded. SB 9.24.26-28
Son of Shurasena; father of Krishna, Balarama and Subhadra. Imprisoned by Kamsa, he bore the newborn Krishna across the river to safety.

Born Pritha, daughter of Shurasena; given in adoption to the childless Kuntibhoja and renamed Kunti. By a sage's boon she could summon any god to father a child, hence Karna and the three eldest Pandavas.
Daughter of Shurasena, sister of Vasudeva; wed to Damaghosha of Chedi and mother of Shishupala.
A childless Bhoja king, cousin of Shurasena; he adopted Pritha, who took his name as Kunti.
Senior wife of Vasudeva; mother of Balarama and Subhadra.

Son of Vasudeva and Devaki; the eighth child, an avatar of Vishnu, spirited to Gokula the night he was born. Counsellor and charioteer of Arjuna, speaker of the Bhagavad Gita. Beyond his eight principal queens (the Ashtabharya) he wed the sixteen thousand one hundred women he freed from the demon Narakasura's captivity, giving each of them honour and a home.
Elder half-brother of Krishna, son of Rohini; wielder of the plough and mace, teacher of both Bhima and Duryodhana.
Sister of Krishna, daughter of Rohini; she eloped with Arjuna at Krishna's urging and became the mother of Abhimanyu.
Princess of Vidarbha, sister of Rukmi; chief queen (patrani) of Krishna, held to be an incarnation of Lakshmi.
Daughter of Satrajit; the fiery queen who rode into battle beside Krishna against the demon Narakasura.
Daughter of the bear-king Jambavan; won when Krishna wrestled Jambavan for the Syamantaka gem. Mother of Samba.
The river Yamuna personified; she wed Krishna after long penance on its banks.
An Avanti princess and Krishna's cousin, whom he carried off from her svayamvara.
Princess of Kosala (also called Satya), won by Krishna when he subdued her father's seven fierce bulls.
A Kekaya princess and Krishna's cousin, given to him by her brothers.
A princess of Madra, won by Krishna at her svayamvara.
Son of Krishna and Rukmini; a rebirth of Kamadeva, the god of love.
Son of Krishna and Jambavati; his prank on the sages drew the curse that destroyed the Yadava race.
Daughter of Rukmi; wife of Pradyumna.
Son of Pradyumna; carried off by Usha, daughter of the asura Bana, and rescued by Krishna.
Daughter of the asura Banasura; she wed Aniruddha.
Great-grandson of Krishna; after the Yadavas destroyed themselves he was made their king, so the line survived.
Daughter of King Raivata; born in an earlier age, she was shrunk to human height to become Balarama's wife.
King of Chedi; husband of Shrutashrava and father of Shishupala.
King of Chedi, cousin of Krishna; born three-eyed and four-armed under a doom that Krishna would kill him, which came to pass at Yudhishthira's rajasuya after his hundredth insult.
A great sage; Drona was born of his seed kept in a vessel (drona).
Preceptor in arms to both Kaurava and Pandava princes; brahmin by birth, warrior by trade, commander of the Kaurava host after Bhishma.
A sage of the Gautama line; father of the twins Kripa and Kripi, born in a clump of reeds and raised in the Kuru court.
Twin of Kripi; a chiranjivi and early teacher of the Kuru princes, he survived the war.
Twin of Kripa; wife of Drona and mother of Ashwatthama.
Son of Drona and Kripi, born with a gem in his brow; a chiranjivi cursed to wander after he slew the Pandava sons in their sleep.
A king of the Nagas (serpent race); father of Ulupi.
King of Manipura; father of Chitrangada, he gave her to Arjuna on the pledge that their son would inherit his throne.
Son of Drupada; a Panchala warrior who died shielding Yudhishthira in the war.
Son of Balarama and Revati.
Son of Balarama and Revati.
Elder son of Virata; among the first great warriors to fall at Kurukshetra.
Son of Virata, slain early in the war.
A princess of the Shibi people; wife of Yudhishthira.
Son of Yudhishthira and Devika.
A princess of Kashi; wife of Bhima.
Son of Bhima and Balandhara.
A princess of Chedi; wife of Nakula.
Son of Nakula and Karenumati.
A princess won by Sahadeva at her svayamvara; his wife.
Son of Sahadeva and Vijaya.
Son of Shishupala; king of Chedi after his father and an ally of the Pandavas in the war.
Son of Dhrishtadyumna, of the Panchala line.
Son of Shalya of Madra, slain in the war.
Son of Shalya of Madra, slain in the war.
Founder-king of Magadha; father of Jarasandha.
The mighty emperor of Magadha, born in two halves joined by the demoness Jara. Rival of Krishna, he was at last torn apart by Bhima. (A namesake also appears among the hundred Kauravas.)
Daughter of Jarasandha; a queen of Kamsa.
Daughter of Jarasandha; a queen of Kamsa. Kamsa's death at Krishna's hands turned their father into Mathura's implacable enemy.
The rishi Shukra, preceptor of the asuras and keeper of the reviving art; father of Devayani.
An asura king; father of Sharmishtha.
A king who won brahmarshi-hood by fierce penance; father of Shakuntala by the apsara Menaka.
An apsara sent to break Vishvamitra's penance; mother of Shakuntala, who was then raised by the sage Kanva.
A Yadava noble, keeper of the Syamantaka gem; father of Satyabhama.
The immortal bear-king of the Ramayan age; Krishna wrestled him for the Syamantaka gem and won his daughter Jambavati.
A thousand-armed asura king and devotee of Shiva; father of Usha.
King Raivata (Kakudmi), who took his daughter Revati to Brahma's realm and returned an age later to a world grown small.
The deva of the sun; an Aditya, son of the devi Aditi and the rishi Kashyap. Father of Karna, whom Kunti bore before her marriage by invoking Surya with a boon she wished to test.
Dharma, the deva of righteousness and lord of justice; father of Yudhishthira, who inherited his unwavering truth.
The deva of the wind; father of the mighty Bhima (and, in the earlier age of the Ramayan, of Hanuman).
King of the devas, wielder of the thunderbolt; an Aditya, son of Aditi and Kashyap, and so a brother of Surya. Father of Arjuna, to whom he later gave celestial weapons.
One of the twin Ashvini Kumaras, devas of dawn and healing; father, by Madri, of Nakula.
One of the twin Ashvini Kumaras, devas of dawn and healing; father, by Madri, of Sahadeva.
Brother of Vasudeva; father of Uddhava.
Brother of Vasudeva, a Vrishni chief.
Brother of Vasudeva, a Vrishni warrior.
Brother of Vasudeva.
Brother of Vasudeva.
Sister of Vasudeva and Kunti; mother of Dantavakra.
Sister of Vasudeva and Kunti; wed to the king of Kekaya.
Sister of Vasudeva and Kunti; mother of Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti.
King of Karusha, son of Shrutadeva; a rebirth of the same doorkeeper of Vishnu as Shishupala, and like him slain by Krishna.
King of Avanti, son of Rajadhidevi; with his brother Anuvinda he fought for the Kauravas (a namesake of one of the hundred Kauravas).
King of Avanti, son of Rajadhidevi and brother of Vinda; a Kaurava ally.
Son of Devabhaga; Krishna's cousin, friend and counsellor, to whom Krishna gave his last teaching.
King of Vidarbha at Kundina; father of Rukmi and of Rukmini.
Prince of Vidarbha, proud brother of Rukmini who opposed her marriage to Krishna; father of Rukmavati.
A Vrishni chief; grandfather of the great warrior Satyaki.
Yuyudhana, grandson of Sini; a mighty Vrishni warrior, pupil of Arjuna and Krishna's charioteer, who fought for the Pandavas.
A Vrishni chief; father of Kritavarma.
Son of Hridika, a Vrishni-Bhoja warrior who fought for the Kauravas and survived the war.
A Yadava elder who bore Krishna and Balarama from Gokula to Mathura; keeper of the Syamantaka gem for a time.
Son of Krishna and Rukmini, a valiant warrior.
Son of Krishna and Satyabhama.
Wife of Nanda; the foster-mother who raised Krishna as her own.
Daughter of Nanda and Yashoda (Ekanamsha); exchanged for the infant Krishna the night he was born.
King of the Nishadas; father of Ekalavya.
Nishada prince who taught himself archery before a clay Drona; Drona claimed his right thumb as guru's fee so none would surpass Arjuna.
The asura king of Pragjyotisha, son of the earth; Krishna slew him and freed the sixteen thousand women he had imprisoned.
King of Pragjyotisha, son of Narakasura; a Kaurava ally who fought from the great elephant Supratika, slain by Arjuna.
Son of Bhagadatta; king of Pragjyotisha after him.
Charioteer and counsellor of Dhritarashtra, son of the suta Gavalgana; granted divine sight by Vyasa, he narrated the war to the blind king.
Son of Vyasa, born radiant and already renounced; the sage who first recited the Bhagavata.
Wife of Brihaspati, guru of the devas; Chandra bore her away, and of that union was born Budha, sparking the war of the devas and asuras.
Guru of the devas (the planet Jupiter), son of the rishi Angiras; husband of Tara.
A mind-born son of Brahma, one of the Saptarishi and eponym of the Angirasa line; father of Brihaspati.
Son of Brihaspati; he went to Shukracharya to learn the art of reviving the dead, and there Devayani loved him in vain.
Favourite among Chandra's twenty-seven wives, the nakshatras, daughters of Daksha.
Son of Surya Deva; progenitor of humankind in this age and father of Ikshvaku, first of the solar kings.
Son of Vaivasvata Manu; founder of the solar dynasty (Suryavamsha) and first king of Kosala at Ayodhya.

Born from his father Yuvanashva's side. Crying for milk, he was given Indra's own index finger to suck, the deva saying mam ayam dhasyati, he shall suck me: hence Mandhata. Emperor of all seven islands, from where the sun rises to where it sets. Also called Trasaddasyu, because thieves trembled at him. SB 9.6.33-37

The king who kept his word past every ruin. Over him Vishvamitra and Vasishtha quarrelled so long that both were turned into birds and fought on as birds for years. Sonless, he begged a son of Varuna against the promise of sacrificing him. SB 9.7.7-8
Emperor whose sixty thousand sons were burnt to ash for disturbing the sage Kapila; generations after Harishchandra.
Wayward son of Sagara, exiled for his cruelty.
Grandson of Sagara who recovered the sacrificial horse; father of Bhagiratha.
Son of Amshuman; by fierce penance he brought the Ganga down from heaven to earth to redeem Sagara's sons, hence the river Bhagirathi.
Dilipa II, also Dirghabahu, son of Khatvanga. The ideal king of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha, whose service of the divine cow Nandini won him his son Raghu. SB 9.10.1
Son of Dilipa; so glorious an emperor that the line is called the Raghuvamsha after him.
Son of Raghu; father of Dasharatha.
King of Kosala at Ayodhya; father of Rama by three queens. His promise to Kaikeyi sent Rama into exile and broke his own heart.
Queen of Dilipa, princess of the Magadha line; mother of Raghu.
Princess who chose Aja at her svayamvara; queen of Aja and mother of Dasharatha.
Chief queen of Dasharatha and mother of Rama; a princess of Dakshina Kosala.
Second queen of Dasharatha, princess of Kekaya; her two boons won Bharata the throne and drove Rama to the forest.
Third queen of Dasharatha; mother of the twins Lakshmana and Shatrughna.
Eldest son of Dasharatha, by Kausalya; the seventh avatar of Vishnu, exiled fourteen years, who slew Ravana to win back Sita.
Son of Dasharatha by Kaikeyi; he refused the throne his mother seized and ruled only as regent for Rama's sandals.
Son of Dasharatha by Sumitra; Rama's devoted brother who followed him into exile and warred at his side.
Youngest son of Dasharatha by Sumitra, twin of Lakshmana; the slayer of the demon Lavana.
Son of Rama and Sita, born in the forest hermitage; twin of Kusha.
Son of Rama and Sita, born in the forest hermitage; twin of Lava. Kusha and Lava sang the Ramayana before their father, not knowing him.
Son of Lakshmana and Urmila (Lakshmana also had a son Angada, a namesake of the vanara prince).
Son of Bharata and Mandavi; he gave his name to Takshashila.
Son of Bharata and Mandavi.
Son of Shatrughna and Shrutakirti; king of Mathura.
Son of Shatrughna and Shrutakirti.
King of Kekaya; father of Kaikeyi and Yudhajit.
Prince of Kekaya, Kaikeyi's brother, whose invitation took Bharata away from Ayodhya at the hour of Dasharatha's death.
King of Videha; father of Janaka and Kushadhvaja. The Janaka kings descend from Nimi, a son of Ikshvaku.
Siradhvaja, the Janaka of the Ramayana. Ploughing the sacrificial ground he turned up Sita from the furrow, sira, and took her as his daughter. SB 9.13.18-19
Younger brother of Janaka, king of Sankashya.
Queen of Janaka; foster-mother of Sita and mother of Urmila.
Found by Janaka in a furrow of the earth (Bhumija) and raised as his daughter; wife of Rama, carried off by Ravana, at last taken back into the earth. Her birth lineage is none but the Earth's.
Daughter of Janaka and Sunayana; wife of Lakshmana, who slept fourteen years in her stead so he could guard Rama night and day.
Daughter of Kushadhvaja; wife of Bharata.
Daughter of Kushadhvaja; wife of Shatrughna.
The self-born creator, source of every lineage in this tree: from his mind-born sons spring the devas, the sages, the rakshasas and, through them, the kings of both the solar and the lunar dynasties.
A mind-born son of Brahma (a Prajapati); grandfather of Ravana through his son Vishrava.
Sage son of Pulastya; father of Kubera by Ilavida and of Ravana and his siblings by the rakshasi Kaikasi.
First wife of Vishrava; mother of Kubera.
Rakshasi wife of Vishrava, daughter of the demon Sumali; mother of Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Shurpanakha and Vibhishana.
Son of Vishrava and Ilavida; the yaksha lord of wealth who first ruled Lanka, until his half-brother Ravana drove him out.
The ten-headed rakshasa king of Lanka; a mighty devotee of Shiva and master of the Vedas whose abduction of Sita brought his doom.
Giant brother of Ravana, cursed to sleep six months at a time; woken for the war, he was slain by Rama.
Sister of Ravana whose courting of Rama and Lakshmana, and the loss of her nose, set the war in motion.
Youngest brother of Ravana; righteous, he deserted to Rama and was crowned king of Lanka after the war.
Mayasura, the great asura architect; father of Mandodari.
Daughter of Mayasura; the wise and virtuous chief queen of Ravana and mother of Indrajit.
Meghanada, son of Ravana and Mandodari; he once defeated Indra himself, hence his name, and was slain by Lakshmana.
Son of Ravana and Mandodari; a colossal warrior slain by Lakshmana.
Young son of Ravana, slain by Hanuman in the burning of Lanka.
Son of Kumbhakarna, killed in the war.
Son of Kumbhakarna, killed in the war.
Wife of Kumbhakarna; a granddaughter of the demon Virochana.
The vanara king of Kishkindha; foster-father of Vali and Sugriva, who were begotten of the gods Indra and Surya.
Elder vanara prince, son of Indra; king of Kishkindha of peerless strength, slain by Rama's arrow to restore Sugriva.
Younger vanara prince, son of Surya; exiled by Vali and restored by Rama, whose army of vanaras he then led to Lanka.
Vanara elder and physician; father of Tara.
Daughter of Sushena; the wise queen of Vali, and after him of Sugriva. Mother of Angada.
Wife of Sugriva.
Son of Vali and Tara; the vanara prince who led Rama's embassy to Ravana.
A vanara chief; the earthly father of Hanuman.

The apsara Punjikasthala, called Managarva in the Puranic account, cursed into the body of a vanara and born a princess of Kishkindha. She and Kesari propitiated Vayu for a son and got Hanuman. Rama 4.66; Puranic Encyclopaedia, Anjana

Son of Kesari and Anjana, begotten by Vayu the wind-god, and himself counted among the devas: a chiranjivi, one of the immortals who never dies, and in the Shaiva reading an avatar of Rudra. He leapt the ocean to Lanka and found Sita, carried the mountain of herbs whole because he could not tell which one healed, and burned the city with his own tail. Rama 1.17, 4.66, 5.1; Shiva Purana 3.20
A rakshasa lord of the elder line of Lanka; father of Kaikasi, whom he gave to the sage Vishrava to sire sons who might rival the devas.
Son of Kusha; a king of the Raghu line.
A king of Kosala descended from Rama.
Disciple of Jaimini, master of the yoga of the mystics, and the teacher from whom Yajnavalkya received that yoga. SB 9.12.3-4
Perfected in yoga and living still, the Puranas say, in the village of Kalapa. At the end of the age of Kali he will begin the solar dynasty again. SB 9.12.5-6

The last of the solar kings the Purana counts as past: he fought at Kurukshetra on the Kaurava side and was killed by Abhimanyu. He and Abhimanyu therefore stand on the same generation, which is what fixes the war's place in this whole tree. SB 9.12.8-9
Daughter of Dasharatha and Kausalya, elder sister of Rama, given in adoption to King Romapada of Anga; wife of the sage Rishyasringa, whose rite granted Dasharatha his sons.

Citraratha, called Romapada, king of Anga. Sonless, he was given his friend Dasharatha's daughter Shanta as his own, and married her to Rishyasringa; by the sage's grace he got a son at last. SB 9.23.7-10
A sage raised without knowledge of women; his coming ended a drought, and his fire-rite gave Dasharatha his four sons. Husband of Shanta.
Son of Ravana, a fierce warrior slain by the vanara Angada.
Son of Ravana, slain by Hanuman.
Three-headed son of Ravana, slain by Hanuman.
Wife of Indrajit (Meghanada), daughter of the naga king Shesha; on his death she followed him onto the pyre.
An elder rakshasa lord; father of Sumali and Malyavan.
Grand old rakshasa, brother of Sumali; the wise elder who counselled Ravana to return Sita and make peace.
Son of Sumali and maternal uncle of Ravana; chief commander of Lanka's army, slain by the vanara Nila.
Rakshasi wife of Vibhishana; she comforted Sita in captivity.
Daughter of Vibhishana and Sarama; the kind rakshasi who watched over Sita and foretold Rama's victory.
Vanara son of Vishwakarma; the architect who built Rama's bridge across the sea to Lanka.
Vanara chief, son of Agni; a commander of Rama's army.
Charioteer of Surya, elder brother of Garuda; father of the vulture-kings Jatayu and Sampati.
Vulture-king, son of Aruna; he gave his life trying to stop Ravana from carrying Sita away.
Vulture-king, elder brother of Jatayu; his far sight found Sita in Lanka for Rama's searchers.
A mind-born son (Prajapati) of Brahma; father of Kashyap.
A mind-born son of Brahma, one of the Saptarishi; father of Chandra (Soma).
A Prajapati; father of the many wives of Kashyap, and so grandfather of the devas, nagas, birds and much else.
The great progenitor rishi; by his many wives, father of the devas (Adityas), the asuras, the nagas and the birds.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Adityas, the devas.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the sun's charioteer Aruna and of Garuda.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the nagas.
Son of Kashyap and Vinata; the mighty eagle who bears Vishnu.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Daitya asuras.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Danava asuras.
Daitya king, son of Kashyap and Diti; slain by Vishnu as Narasimha for tormenting his devotee son Prahlada.
Daitya, son of Kashyap and Diti; slain by Vishnu as the boar Varaha.
Son of Hiranyakashipu; a supreme devotee of Vishnu whom no torment could shake.
Son of Prahlada; a Daitya king, father of Bali.
Mahabali, son of Virochana; the generous asura emperor whom Vishnu, as the dwarf Vamana, measured out of the three worlds. His line runs on to Banasura of the Mahabharat age (Usha's father).
King of the nagas, son of Kashyap and Kadru; the serpent-rope of the ocean's churning.
A naga king, son of Kashyap and Kadru; his bite would one day slay Parikshit.
Ananta, the endless serpent, son of Kashyap and Kadru, on whom Vishnu reclines.
Goddess of speech and wisdom, consort of Brahma; mother of his mind-born sons.
A mind-born son of Brahma, a Prajapati and Saptarishi; father of Shukracharya, guru of the asuras.
A mind-born son of Brahma, chief of the Saptarishi and family priest of the Ikshvaku kings; forefather of the line of Parashara and Vyasa.
Son of Vasishtha and father of Parashara; of the Vasishtha line.
Son of Pururavas; founder of the Kanyakubja (Kaushika) branch of the lunar line.
King of Kanyakubja of the Kaushika (Amavasu) branch of the lunar line; father of the sage-king Vishvamitra.
Sanjna, daughter of Vishvakarma and chief wife of Surya; mother of Vaivasvata Manu, Yama, Yami and the Ashvin twins.
The shadow-image of Sandhya, second wife of Surya; mother of Shani, Tapati and Savarni Manu.
Daughter of Surya and Sandhya, twin of Yama; the river-goddess Yamuna.
Son of Surya and Chaya; the slow, stern planet Saturn.
Daughter of Surya and Chaya; wed King Samvarana, an ancestress of the Kurus.
Son of Surya and Chaya; the Manu of a coming age (Savarni Manu).
One of the twenty-seven nakshatras, daughters of Daksha and wives of Chandra.
One of the twenty-seven nakshatras, daughters of Daksha and wives of Chandra.

Wife of Vaivasvata Manu; mother of Ila and of the Manu sons who founded the earth's royal houses.
Son of Manu; his line held Anarta and Kusasthali (Dvaraka's site).
Son of Manu; forebear of a solar branch.
Son of Manu; a king cursed to live as a lizard for a gift gone wrong.
Son of Manu.
Son of Manu; forebear of the Vaishya kings.
Son of Manu, made a shudra for slaying his guru's cow.
A mighty son of Kashyap and Diti, of adamantine body; father, by Varangi, of Tarakasura.
Wife of Vajranga; mother of Tarakasura.
Asura son of Vajranga and Varangi, boon-armoured against all but a son of Shiva; slain at last by Kartikeya. Father of the three lords of Tripura.
Son of Tarakasura; a lord of the flying triple-city Tripura.
Son of Tarakasura; a lord of Tripura.
Son of Tarakasura; a lord of Tripura, the three cities burnt by Shiva.
Foremost of the Danava sons of Kashyap and Danu; wed Simhika and fathered Rahu.
A Danava son of Danu, slain by Indra with sea-foam.
A Danava sorcerer-king, son of Danu; foe of Pradyumna.
Aditya lord of the waters and cosmic order.
Aditya of friendship and contracts, paired with Varuna.
Aditya of custom, patron of marriage and the ancestors.
Aditya of fortune and inherited share.
Aditya of roads, herds and safe journeys.
The dwarf Aditya, avatar of Vishnu, who measured the three worlds from Bali.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of cattle, the wish-granting cows.
The wish-fulfilling cow, daughter of Surabhi.
Divine cow, daughter of Surabhi, kept by the sage Vasishtha.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the birds of prey.
Daughter of Tamra; mother of hawks and falcons.
Daughter of Tamra; mother of kites and vultures.
Daughter of Tamra; mother of the vultures.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the apsaras.
Foremost of the apsaras, daughter of Muni.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of fierce Danavas.
Danava son of Danayus (or Tvashtar); the drought-serpent slain by Indra with the vajra.
A Danava son of Danayus.
Daughter of Diti (sister of Hiranyakashipu); wife of Viprachitti, mother of Rahu.
Son of Viprachitti and Simhika; the severed asura-head that swallows sun and moon at eclipses.
A great naga king, son of Kashyap and Kadru.
A naga of Kadru's line (namesake of Indra's elephant).
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Gandharvas.
King of the Gandharvas (Angaraparna); Arjuna bested him on the Ganga and he gave the Pandavas the Chakshushi lore and celestial horses.
A Gandharva master of music, singer in Indra's court.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; a mother of serpents, and the sea-nagi who tested Hanuman's wit on the leap to Lanka.
The hundred-hooded serpent of the Yamuna, quelled when Krishna danced upon his hoods.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the beasts of the wild.
Daughter of Krodhavasha; mother of lions, tigers and the great cats.
Daughter of Krodhavasha; mother of the monkeys and the horses.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of trees, creepers and grasses.
Lord of the forest trees, child of Ira; the standing green world.
King of the Kuru line who wed Tapati, Surya's daughter; father of Kuru, the dynasty's eponym.
Son of Sharyati; his realm Anarta held the coast where Dvaraka would rise.
Son of Bhrigu; the aged sage restored to youth by the Ashvins, husband of Sukanya. The rejuvenating tonic Chyavanprash, which the Ashvins first prepared for him, is named after him.
Daughter of King Sharyati; devoted wife of the sage Chyavana.
Bhargava sage of the fire of wrath, born of the Bhrigu line through Chyavana.
Bhargava sage; wed Satyavati of Gadhi's house, father of Jamadagni.
Daughter of King Gadhi and sister of Vishvamitra; wife of Richika.
Bhargava rishi, son of Richika; husband of Renuka, father of Parashurama.
Wife of Jamadagni, mother of Parashurama; a devoted and much-tried queen.
The axe-wielding Bhargava, avatar of Vishnu; a chiranjivi who taught Bhishma, Drona and Karna and ranged across the ages.
Aditya, the divine artificer (Vishvakarma); father of Sanjna (Sandhya), Surya's wife.
Three-headed son of Tvashtar, priest to the devas, beheaded by Indra.
Wife of Atri, a paragon of virtue; mother of Dattatreya, Durvasa and Chandra.
Son of Atri and Anasuya; an avatar uniting Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
Son of Atri and Anasuya; the wrath-swift sage whose boon gave Kunti her deva-sons.
Severed body of the eclipse-asura, brother of Rahu; the descending shadow-node.
Asura son of Simhika who, with Ilvala, preyed on guests until the sage Agastya digested him.
Asura son of Simhika; brother of Vatapi.
Wife of Hiranyakashipu, mother of Prahlada; kept safe by Narada while her lord warred with heaven.
Brother of Prahlada, son of Hiranyakashipu.
Brother of Prahlada, son of Hiranyakashipu.
Brother of Prahlada, son of Hiranyakashipu.
Daitya son of Hiranyaksha (or of Shiva's sweat), the blind asura slain by Shiva.
Wife of Bali; queen of the generous asura emperor.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Yakshas and Rakshasas.
Progenitor of the yakshas, the guardian nature-spirits of wealth.
Progenitor of the rakshasas, the night-wandering kind.
The pot-born sage, son of Mitra and Varuna; who drank the ocean, humbled the Vindhya, and digested the asura Vatapi. Husband of Lopamudra.
Princess fashioned for the sage Agastya; his learned wife and a hymn-seer in her own right.
Twin of Divodasa in the royal Panchala line; also told as Brahma-born (the divine ray). Famed as the wife of Gautama, cursed and later redeemed.
Gautama Maharishi, of the Angirasa gotra (descended from Utathya, son of Angiras). Husband of Ahalya.
Son of Gautama and Ahalya; purohita of King Janaka of Videha.
Son of Gautama and Ahalya; the son who deliberated so long he spared a rash act (Mahabharata).

King of Nishadha, son of Virasena. Master of horses and of cookery, and beloved of Damayanti before either had seen the other. Possessed by Kali, he gambled his kingdom away to his brother Pushkara, abandoned Damayanti in the forest, and lived disfigured as Bahuka, charioteer and cook to Rituparna of Ayodhya, until the science of horses he traded for the science of dice gave him both back. MBh 3.50-78

Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhima, who loved Nala on report alone and knew him at her svayamvara among four devas wearing his face, because only his feet touched the ground. Abandoned in the forest, she made her way back by a brahmin's recognition and drew her husband out of hiding with a riddling verse. MBh 3.50-78
Also called Indrasena; daughter of Nala and Damayanti, wife of Mudgala.
Eponym of the Maudgalya gotra: the Brahmin line of Mudgala’s descendants, distinct from the royal Panchala line carried by Vadhryasva.
Somaka’s eldest son; offered in sacrifice, per the Mahabharata, so that Somaka might gain a hundred sons.
Asura brother of Vatapi; the pair who preyed on guests until Agastya digested Vatapi.
Wife of Vasishtha; the star Alcor, paired with him as the archetypal devoted couple.
Also Indrani/Pulomaja; queen of the devas, wife of Indra.
Daughter of Indra; wed to Shukracharya.
Daughter of Indra; wed to Kartikeya (Skanda).
Wife of Bhrigu; mother of Chyavana and Shukracharya.
Naga elder; per the Mahabharata, kin who revived Bhima with nectar in the naga realm.
God of love, mind-born of Brahma. (Later reborn as Pradyumna, Krishna’s son.)
Goddess of desire; daughter of Daksha, wife of Kamadeva.
Eldest of Ikshvaku's hundred sons. Banished for eating a hare from the sacrificial offering, hence Shashada, the hare-eater; recalled to the throne at his father's death. SB 9.6.6-8
Fought the demons for the devas mounted on Indra, who had taken the form of a bull: seated on its hump he is Kakutstha, and as the vehicle of Indra, Indravaha. SB 9.6.11-15
Son of Puranjaya. SB 9.6.16
Fifth of the solar kings. Not Vena's son Prithu, for whom the earth is named. SB 9.6.16
Son of Vishvagandhi. Not Chandra Deva of the lunar line. SB 9.6.17
Built Shravasti Puri, the city that kept his name. SB 9.6.20
Killed the demon Dhundhu with twenty-one thousand sons at his side, and took the name Dhundhumara, slayer of Dhundhu. All but three of the sons burned in the fire the demon breathed. SB 9.6.21-24
One of the three sons who survived Dhundhu's fire, with Kapilashva and Bhadrashva. SB 9.6.23-24
Son of Haryashva. Not the rakshasa Nikumbha of Lanka. SB 9.6.24

A hundred wives and no son. The sages held an Indra-yajna for him in the forest; thirsty in the night he drank the consecrated water himself, and in time bore the child from his own right side. SB 9.6.25-32

Given Narmada, sister of the Nagas, by her serpent brothers; she carried him down to Rasatala where, empowered by Vishnu, he killed the Gandharvas. Whoever remembers it is safe from snakes. SB 9.7.2-3; RV 6.20.10
Bears his great-grandfather's epithet as his name. In the Rigveda he is called ardhadeva, half-god, a word used of no one else. SB 9.7.4; RV 4.42.8-9

Cursed by his own father into a chandala for carrying off a brahmin's bride at her wedding. Vishvamitra sent him bodily to heaven; the devas threw him back; Vishvamitra stopped him mid-fall, and he hangs there yet, head downward. SB 9.7.5-6

The son promised to Varuna before his birth and deferred past every excuse; he took bow and arrows to the forest to stay alive, and came back six years later having bought Shunahshepha in his place. SB 9.7.9-20
Built Champapuri, which later became the capital of Anga. SB 9.8.1
Driven out by his enemies, he died in the forest. His pregnant widow was poisoned by her co-wives but the child was born alive, carrying the poison: sa-gara. SB 9.8.2-5
Tried to bring the Ganga down to redeem Sagara's sons and died without succeeding. Not the Dilipa of the Raghuvamsha, who is four generations below Khatvanga. SB 9.9.1
Son of Bhagiratha. SB 9.9.16

King of Ayodhya, and the friend of Nala. He gave Nala the akshahridaya, the heart of the dice, and took from him the ashvavidya, the science of horses. Nala served in his kitchen and at his reins under the name Bahuka. SB 9.9.16-17; MBh 3.65-70
Not Sudasa of Panchala, nor the Rigvedic Sudas Paijavana of the Bharatas. SB 9.9.18

Also Mitrasaha. Cursed by Vasishtha into a rakshasa; in that state he devoured a brahmin, and the widow cursed him to die at his next embrace. Twelve years sonless, he let Vasishtha beget his heir on his queen Madayanti. SB 9.9.20-38
Carried for years and finally born when Vasishtha struck his mother's womb with a stone, ashman. SB 9.9.38
Survived Parashurama's purge of the kshatriyas screened by a ring of women, hence Narikavacha, armoured in women; and because the kshatriyas began again from him, Mulaka, the root. SB 9.9.39-40
Son of Balika, and not the father of Rama. SB 9.9.41
Fought at the devas' side and won; offered a boon, he asked only how long he had to live, was told a few moments, left heaven at once and gave those moments entirely to Hari. SB 9.9.41-49
Son of Nishadha. SB 9.12.1
Said to be born of the sun's effulgence. SB 9.12.2
The last king the Raghuvamsha follows. SB 9.12.5
Son of Prasenajit. Not Takshaka the Naga who killed Parikshit. SB 9.12.7

Second son of Ikshvaku. He would not wait for Vasishtha to finish Indra's sacrifice before beginning his own, and the two cursed each other's bodies to fall. From his preserved body, churned by the sages, Janaka was born. SB 9.13.1-11

Born of no womb, from the churning of his father's body: hence Vaideha, the bodiless-born, and Mithi, the churned, and Mithila for the city he founded. Every king of this line is called Janaka after him. SB 9.13.12-13
Not Shunahshepha, whom Vishvamitra adopted under the same name. SB 9.13.14
Not Maru of Kalapa in the Ikshvaku line. SB 9.13.15
A self-realized king; his cousin Khandikya was expert in ritual, and the two exchanged what each lacked. SB 9.13.21-22
Brother of Kritadhvaja. SB 9.13.21
Son of Mitadhvaja, master of ritual, who fled Keshidhvaja and later taught him karma-kanda in exchange for knowledge of the self. SB 9.13.22

Yadava emperor of the world, a great mystic who held fourteen jewels; ten thousand wives and a lakh of sons by each. His daughter Bindumati married Mandhata of the solar line, and their two houses meet in her. SB 9.23.31-32

Daughter of the Yadava emperor Shashabindu; queen of Mandhata, mother of Purukutsa, Ambarisha and Muchukunda and of fifty daughters. The cleanest marriage between the solar and lunar lines in the Puranas. SB 9.6.38
Son of Mandhata, and the most prominent of the three; accepted as son by his own grandfather Yuvanashva. Not Ambarisha the devotee, of Nabhaga's branch, whom Durvasa cursed. SB 9.7.1

Son of Mandhata. He guarded the devas through a war of ages until Kartikeya came to relieve him, and when they offered him any boon but liberation he asked for sleep, and that whoever woke him should burn. He slept in a cave through the ages. Krishna led Kalayavana into that cave; Kalayavana kicked the sleeping man, and was ash before he understood. Then Muchukunda, who had lain down in his father's age, opened his eyes on Vishnu. SB 9.6.38, 10.51
Son of Ambarisha. SB 9.7.1
With Ambarisha and Yauvanashva, one of the three most prominent in Mandhata's line. SB 9.7.1

One of the fifty daughters of Mandhata and Bindumati. The Puranas name none of them individually, so she stands here for all fifty, who chose Saubhari together and then quarrelled over him, each certain he was hers alone. SB 9.6.38-44

Deep in the Yamuna at his austerity he watched a pair of fish mate, and desire took him. He asked Mandhata for a daughter; the king, seeing grey hair and a trembling head, said only that his daughters chose for themselves. So Saubhari made himself young, and all fifty chose him. By his mantras he built each of them a palace, and in his own words: I became the husband of fifty wives, and in each of them I begot one hundred sons, and thus my family increased to five thousand. Then he saw what the fish had cost him, took vanaprastha, and his wives followed him. SB 9.6.39-55
Sister of the Nagas, given to Purukutsa by her serpent brothers at Vasuki's bidding, and the river of that name. SB 9.7.2

A brahmin of Garga's line, mocked as impotent by Syala in the Yadava assembly. He went to the western sea and lived twelve years on iron filings until Shiva granted him a son who would break the Yadavas. HV 58; VP 5.23
The apsara who took the form of a cowherd woman and bore Gargya his son. Called Rambha in some recensions. HV 58

Born of Gargya and the apsara Gopali, and raised by the childless king of the Yavanas. Narada pointed him at Mathura and he came with thirty million soldiers. Krishna, carrying no weapon, ran from him into a mountain cave, where Kalayavana kicked a sleeping man he took for Krishna, and Muchukunda's first waking glance burned him to ash. SB 10.50-51
The childless king of the Yavanas, Gargya's friend, who raised Kalayavana as his own. VP 5.23
A starving brahmin who sold his middle son to be Harishchandra's sacrifice, and took a further fee to hold the knife himself. SB 9.7.20; AB 7.13-16

Bought by Rohita to die in his place, he praised the devas from the stake until his bonds fell away. Vishvamitra adopted him as Devarata, god-given, over the protests of his own sons. His brothers were Shunahpuccha and Shunolangula. SB 9.7.20-26; AB 7.13-18
Eldest son of Ajigarta, whom his father would not sell. AB 7.15
Youngest son of Ajigarta, whom his mother would not give. AB 7.15
Son of Puru. Not Parikshit's son. SB 9.20.1
Ten sons by the apsara Ghritachi: Riteyu, Kaksheyu, Sthandileyu, Kriteyuka, Jaleyu, Sannateyu, Dharmeyu, Satyeyu, Vrateyu and Vaneyu. SB 9.20.3-4
Eldest of Raudrashva's ten. SB 9.20.5
Three sons: Sumati, Dhruva and Apratiratha, whose son Kanva raised Shakuntala. SB 9.20.6
Son of Rantinava. SB 9.20.6

Son of Apratiratha, kshatriya-born and a brahmin by life. He found the infant Shakuntala in the forest where Menaka had left her, brought her to his ashram and raised her; it was under his roof that Dushyanta met her. SB 9.20.6-11
Son of Kanva; his sons, headed by Praskanna, were all brahmins. SB 9.20.7

Bharata's sacrifices gave him no worthy heir, and Bharadvaja, the son Brihaspati begot on Mamata, was given to him instead: given away he is Vitatha, the one who was otherwise. The same sage appears in this tree in his own right, in the Angirasa line, as the father of Drona. SB 9.20.37-38
Five sons: Brihatkshatra, Jaya, Mahavirya, Nara and Garga. SB 9.21.19
Eldest of Manyu's five. SB 9.21.19, 9.21.21
Son of Manyu. SB 9.21.19
Son of Nara; father of Guru and of Rantideva. SB 9.21.1

He gave away his own food until he and his household fasted. After forty-eight days without even water, food came, and with it a brahmin guest, then a shudra, then a stranger, then a thirsty man for the last of the water: he gave each of them everything, and asked for nothing but that all beings be free of suffering. SB 9.21.2-18
Brother of Rantideva. SB 9.21.1
Son of Manyu; his line, kshatriya by birth, became brahmins. SB 9.21.19, 9.21.31
Son of Ajamidha by Nalini. Not Nila the vanara commander. SB 9.21.32
Eldest son of Kuru, who left no sons. SB 9.22.4, 9.22.9
Son of Kuru, from whom the line runs to Uparichara Vasu and thence to Magadha, Matsya and Chedi. SB 9.22.4-6
Son of Kuru. The Bhagavata runs the Kuru succession through him; this tree keeps the Mahabharata's line through Viduratha, and both are recorded. SB 9.22.4, 9.22.9
Youngest son of Kuru. Not Nishadha of the solar line, nor Nala's kingdom. SB 9.22.4
Not Chyavana the Bhargava sage, nor Chyavana of Panchala. SB 9.22.5

King of Chedi, called Uparichara, the sky-goer, for the crystal chariot Indra gave him. His sons became the kings of Chedi, of Magadha and of Matsya, and his daughter, born of a fish, became Satyavati. SB 9.22.6; MBh 1.57
Queen of Uparichara Vasu. MBh 1.57
Son of Uparichara Vasu, a king of Chedi. SB 9.22.6
Son of Uparichara Vasu, a king of Chedi. SB 9.22.6
Son of Uparichara Vasu, and the king from whom the Chedis take their name. SB 9.22.6

An apsara cursed into a fish in the Yamuna. She swallowed the seed of Uparichara Vasu and bore twins: the boy who founded the Matsya kingdom, and the girl Satyavati, who was raised by fishermen. MBh 1.57
Born of the fish with his sister Satyavati; the Matsya kingdom keeps his name. Also counted among Uparichara Vasu's sons at SB 9.22.6. MBh 1.57
Son of Ayus, from whom the kings of Kashi descend. SB 9.17.1

Son of Ayus. Indra gave him the kingdom of heaven for his help against the demons; his five hundred sons would not give it back, and Brihaspati's rites unmade their intelligence until Indra took it. SB 9.17.1, 9.17.10-17
Son of Ayus. His line: Rabhasa, Gambhira, Akriya, Brahmavit. SB 9.17.1, 9.17.11
Son of Ayus. His line: Shuddha, Shuchi, Chitrakrit, Shantaraja. Not Anena of the solar line. SB 9.17.1, 9.17.11
Three sons: Kashya, Kusha and Gritsamada. SB 9.17.2
The king from whom Kashi takes its name. SB 9.17.4
Who brought medicine into the world: the founder of Ayurveda, and a shaktyavesha incarnation of Vasudeva. Merely remembering him, the Purana says, quiets disease. SB 9.17.4
King of Kashi. One of the four to whom Yayati's daughter Madhavi was lent, and by her the father of Pratardana. Not Divodasa of Panchala. SB 9.17.5; MBh 5.113
Son of Divodasa of Kashi by Madhavi; called also Shatrujit, Vatsa, Ritadhvaja and Kuvalayashva. SB 9.17.5-6; MBh 5.113
Reigned, the Purana says, sixty-six thousand years, and no other king enjoyed the earth so long in the vigour of youth. SB 9.17.6-7
Son of Druhyu. SB 9.23.14
The king from whom Gandhara takes its name. SB 9.23.15
A hundred sons, who took the north of India and ruled there. SB 9.23.15-16
Eldest of Anu's three sons, with Chakshu and Pareshnu. SB 9.23.1
Son of Srinjaya of the Anu line. SB 9.23.2
Two sons, Ushinara and Titikshu, and from them the two great Anu branches: Madra and Kekaya on one side, Anga and Karna's throne on the other. SB 9.23.2
King of the Bhojas. One of the four to whom Yayati's daughter Madhavi was lent, and by her the father of Shibi. SB 9.23.2-3; MBh 5.114
Brother of Ushinara; the Anga line descends from him. SB 9.23.2-4

Son of Ushinara by Madhavi. A hawk claimed a dove that had taken refuge with him, and rather than give up the one who trusted him he cut flesh from his own body to pay the weight. Four sons: Vrishadarbha, Sudhira, Madra and Kekaya. SB 9.23.3; MBh 3.131, 5.114
Son of Ushinara. SB 9.23.3
Son of Ushinara. SB 9.23.3
Son of Ushinara. Not Daksha the Prajapati. SB 9.23.3
Son of Shibi. SB 9.23.3
Son of Shibi. SB 9.23.3
Son of Shibi, and the king from whom Madra takes its name. SB 9.23.3
Son of Shibi, called atma-tattva-vit, knower of the truth of the self; the Kekaya kingdom keeps his name. SB 9.23.3
Emperor of the world in the Anu line, and sonless. Not Bali the Daitya, Prahlada's grandson. SB 9.23.4-5
Queen of Bali. Six sons by the sage Dirghatamas, each of whom took a kingdom in the east. SB 9.23.5-6

The blind sage of the Rigveda, son of Mamata and Utathya, and by Bali's queen the father of Anga, Vanga, Kalinga, Suhma, Pundra and Odra: six kings and six kingdoms of the east. His own son by the maid Ushij was Kakshivan. SB 9.23.5; RV 1.140-164
Eldest of the six; the Anga kingdom, whose throne Duryodhana would one day give to Karna, keeps his name. SB 9.23.5-6
One of the six sons of Dirghatamas by Bali's queen. SB 9.23.5

Three sons: Brihadratha, Brihatkarma and Brihadbhanu. SB 9.23.10-11
Eldest son of Prithulaksha. Not Brihadratha of Magadha. SB 9.23.11
Not Jayadratha of Sindhu, Dushala's husband. SB 9.23.11-12
Son of Jayadratha by his wife Sambhuti. SB 9.23.12

Sonless, he adopted Dushyanta out of the Puru line; Dushyanta later went home to claim his own throne, which is why the Puru succession reads unbroken. SB 9.23.17-18
Eldest of Yadu's four sons; the Haihayas descend from him. SB 9.23.20-21
Third son of Yadu. Not Nala of Nishadha, nor Nala the vanara. SB 9.23.20
Fourth son of Yadu. SB 9.23.20
Three sons: Mahahaya, Renuhaya and Haihaya. SB 9.23.21
The king from whom the Haihayas take their name. SB 9.23.21
Son of Netra, a Haihaya king. Not Pritha, the Pandavas' mother. SB 9.23.22
Whose city Mahishmati stood on the Narmada. SB 9.23.22
Two sons: Durmada and Dhanaka. SB 9.23.22-23
Four sons: Kritavirya, Kritagni, Kritavarma and Kritauja. SB 9.23.23

Emperor of all seven islands, who received the eight mystic perfections from Dattatreya and ruled eighty-five thousand years with his strength and memory unbroken. He took Jamadagni's cow, and Parashurama killed him for it, and then killed the kshatriyas twenty-one times over. Of his thousand sons five survived. SB 9.23.24-27
One of the five sons of Kartavirya Arjuna who survived Parashurama. SB 9.23.27
A surviving son of Kartavirya Arjuna. Not Shurasena the Yadava, Vasudeva's father. SB 9.23.27

A hundred sons, the Talajanghas, and every kshatriya of that house was destroyed by Sagara with the power Aurva Rishi had given him. SB 9.23.28
Eldest of Talajangha's hundred. SB 9.23.29
Son of Rushadru in the Kroshtu line. Not Chitraratha the Gandharva. SB 9.23.31
Foremost among Shashabindu's sons, with Prithukirti. SB 9.23.33
Performer of a hundred horse sacrifices. SB 9.23.33
Five sons: Purujit, Rukma, Rukmeshu, Prithu and Jyamagha. SB 9.23.34

Sonless, and too afraid of his barren queen Shaibya to take another wife. He brought a captive girl home on his chariot, and when Shaibya demanded to know who sat in her seat he said, your daughter-in-law. The devas made the words true: Shaibya bore Vidarbha, and Vidarbha grew up and married the girl. SB 9.23.34-38
Born to Jyamagha and Shaibya by the mercy of the devas; three sons, Kusha, Kratha and Romapada. The Vidarbha kingdom keeps his name. SB 9.23.38, 9.24.1
Son of Vidarbha; the Vrishni line runs through him. SB 9.24.1, 9.24.3
Son of Kratha. SB 9.24.3
Son of Kunti of the Kratha line, generations above the Vrishni for whom the clan is named. SB 9.24.3
The Dasharhas take their name from him. SB 9.24.3
Son of Dasharatha of the Yadava line. Not Shakuni of Gandhara. SB 9.24.5
Queen of Jyamagha, barren and jealous, whose sharp question became a blessing: she bore Vidarbha, and the captive girl she had objected to became her daughter-in-law. SB 9.23.35-38

Son of Vidarbha and the favourite of that house. Not Romapada of Anga. SB 9.24.1
From him the Caidyas. A second derivation of Chedi beside Cedipa of the Uparichara Vasu line; the Bhagavata gives both. SB 9.24.2
Son of Kuruvasha. Not Anu the son of Yayati. SB 9.24.5
Seven sons: Bhajamana, Bhaji, Divya, Vrishni, Devavridha, Andhaka and Mahabhoja, and the branches of the whole Yadava house run from them. SB 9.24.6-8
Son of Satvata. Six sons by two wives: Nimloci, Kinkana and Dhrishti; Shatajit, Sahasrajit and Ayutajit. SB 9.24.7-8

Son of Satvata. Of him and his son Babhru the old verse says that Babhru is the best of men and Devavridha the equal of the devas, and that fourteen thousand and sixty-five of their descendants attained liberation by their company. SB 9.24.7-11
Son of Satvata, an exceedingly religious king, from whom the Bhoja kings descend. SB 9.24.7, 9.24.11
Son of Satvata; four sons, Kukura, Bhajamana, Shuchi and Kambalabarhisha, and from Kukura the line runs to Ahuka, Devaka and Ugrasena. Not Andhaka the Daitya. SB 9.24.7, 9.24.19
Son of Devavridha, praised with his father in an old verse. SB 9.24.9-10
Eldest of Andhaka's four sons, with Bhajamana, Shuchi and Kambalabarhisha. SB 9.24.19
Whose friend was the gandharva Tumburu. SB 9.24.20

Daughter of Punarvasu, sister of Ahuka. SB 9.24.21

Son of Vrishni; father of Shini and Anamitra. Not Yudhajit of Kekaya. SB 9.24.12
Son of Yudhajit. Three sons: Nighna, a second Shini, and Vrishni. SB 9.24.12-14
Son of Anamitra; his sons were Satrajita and Prasena. SB 9.24.12-13
Son of Anamitra, and father of Shvaphalka and Chitraratha. SB 9.24.14
Son of Nighna, brother of Satrajit; he wore the Syamantaka jewel to the hunt and was killed by a lion. SB 9.24.13; 10.56
Son of Vrishni; by his wife Gandini the father of Akrura and twelve more, and a daughter Suchara. SB 9.24.15-18
Wife of Shvaphalka, mother of Akrura. SB 9.24.15

Of the Amavasu branch of the lunar line. Not Bhima the Pandava, nor Bhima of Vidarbha. VP 4.7; SB 9.15.2
Who drank the whole of the Ganga in one sip when her waters flooded his sacrifice, and released her again from his ear: hence she is Jahnavi, daughter of Jahnu. SB 9.15.3
Son of Jahnu. Not Puru the son of Yayati. SB 9.15.3

King of Nishadha, father of Nala. MBh 3.50
Brother of Nala, who won the kingdom from him at dice with Dvapara riding the throw, and lost it back on a single cast when Nala returned. MBh 3.56, 3.78
Son of Nala and Damayanti; with his sister he was sent to Vidarbha by the charioteer Varshneya when their parents' fortune turned. MBh 3.59
King of Vidarbha, long childless, who got his four children by the grace of the sage Damana; father of Damayanti. Not Bhima the Pandava. MBh 3.50

Daughter of Yayati, given not in marriage but in loan: her blessing was that she recovered her maidenhood after each birth and that her sons would be kings. Galava lent her to three kings for two hundred white horses each and to Vishvamitra for the last two hundred, and she bore Vasumanas, Pratardana, Shibi and Ashtaka. Offered a svayamvara afterwards she chose the forest instead and lived as a deer lives. When Yayati fell out of heaven for pride, these four grandsons gave him the merit of their sacrifices and raised him back. MBh 5.113-121
King of Ayodhya, the first of the four to whom Madhavi was lent, and by her the father of Vasumanas. MBh 5.113
Son of Haryashva of Ayodhya by Madhavi, renowned for giving; one of the four grandsons who lifted Yayati back to heaven. MBh 5.113, 5.118
Son of Vishvamitra by Madhavi, renowned for his sacrifices; one of the four grandsons who lifted Yayati back to heaven. MBh 5.115, 5.118

Son of Hanuman, born without a mother's womb. Cooling himself in the sea after burning Lanka, Hanuman shed a drop of sweat; a makara swallowed it and conceived, and when the fish was cut open the child inside was part vanara and part reptile. Ahiravana's people raised him and set him to guard the gates of Patala, where his own father, come to rescue Rama and Lakshmana, had to fight him without knowing him. Hanuman, who had been a brahmachari since birth, saw the truth in dhyana, and afterwards gave him Patala to rule. Krittivasi and Ananda Ramayanas; Ramakien, where he is Macchanu

The makara of the ocean who swallowed a drop of Hanuman's sweat as he cooled himself after burning Lanka, and conceived Makardhwaja by it. The Indian retellings leave her unnamed and call her only the makara, so she carries the creature's name here; the Thai Ramakien names her Suvannamaccha and makes her a mermaid, and Ravana's daughter. Krittivasi Ramayana; Ramakien

Rakshasa king of Patala, a sorcerer who carried Rama and Lakshmana off in their sleep to sacrifice them to his goddess. He raised the fish-born Makardhwaja and made him his gatekeeper, and Hanuman killed him. The retellings differ over whether he is Ravana's son or his brother, and often pair him with Mahiravana. Krittivasi Ramayana; Ananda Ramayana

Son of Angada, and so Vali's grandson: the Brahmanda Purana carries the house of Kishkindha one generation past the war, where Valmiki leaves it. Not Dhruva the son of Uttanapada, who became the pole star. Brahmanda Purana 3.7.220
A vanara chief of Kishkindha, one of the captains Sugriva sent out to search for Sita, and the father of Ruma. Rama 4.39; Brahmanda Purana 3.7.221

The architect of the devas, who built Lanka for Kubera and the chariots and weapons of heaven. His son Nala inherited the craft, which is how a bridge of floating stone reached across the sea. Rama 6.22
The deva of fire, who carries the offering. Father of the vanara Nila, whose effulgence the epic says was his father's. Rama 1.17
King of Avanti, husband of Rajadhidevi and father of Vinda and Anuvinda. SB 9.24.42

Queen of Saudasa Kalmashapada. Her husband cursed to die at his next embrace, she bore his heir Ashmaka to Vasishtha by his own leave, and carried the child for years until Vasishtha struck her womb with a stone. Also called Damayanti in some recensions, and not to be confused with Damayanti of Vidarbha. SB 9.9.33-38
First queen of Sagara, and mother of the sixty thousand who dug the ocean-trench and were burned to ash by Kapila. SB 9.8.8-13
Second queen of Sagara, mother of Asamanjas, through whom the solar line continued. SB 9.8.14-16

Son of Nabhaga, emperor of the world and the great devotee. Durvasa, offended over a broken fast, loosed a demon from his own hair at him; the Sudarshana chakra burned the demon and chased the sage through every world until he came back and begged pardon of the king he had wronged. Three sons: Virupa, Ketuman and Shambhu. SB 9.4-9.5, 9.6.1
Son of Ambarisha. SB 9.6.1
Son of Virupa. SB 9.6.1
Sonless; at his request the sage Angira begot sons in his wife's womb, and they were counted to both houses, Angirasa and Rathitara at once. SB 9.6.1-3
Son of Ambarisha. SB 9.6.1
Son of Ambarisha. SB 9.6.1

Chief of the cowherds of Gokula, husband of Yashoda, and Krishna's foster father. The child was carried across the Yamuna to him the night he was born, and his own newborn daughter carried back in exchange. Not Nanda the Kaurava, who shares the name. BhP 10.3-10.5
King of Karusha, husband of Shrutadeva and father of Dantavakra. SB 9.24.37

The sons of Sudyumna (Ila’s male phase).
One marriage standing for fifty. Their five thousand sons are named nowhere. SB 9.6.52
Garga's son was Shini and Shini's son Gargya, kshatriya-born and brahmin by practice. SB 9.21.31
The fish-born twins. MBh 1.57
The second of Madhavi's four. MBh 5.113

Alarka's line runs on through Santati, Sunitha, Niketana, Dharmaketu, Satyaketu, Dhrishtaketu, Sukumara, Vitihotra, Bharga and Bhargabhumi, all of Kashi. Kashiraja, father of Amba, Ambika and Ambalika, stands at its end. SB 9.17.8-9
The texts fall silent between Gandhara and Subala, father of Gandhari and Shakuni. SB 9.23.15
Madra's line runs unnamed down to Dyutimanta, father of Shalya and Madri. SB 9.23.3
Kekaya's line runs unnamed down to Ashvapati, father of Kaikeyi and Yudhajit. SB 9.23.3
Niyoga: begotten for the sonless Bali, and counted as his. SB 9.23.5-6
Between Vidarbha and Bhishmaka of Kundina, father of Rukmi and Rukmini, the texts name no one. SB 9.24.1
Between Matsya, the fish-born son of Uparichara Vasu, and Virata of the Matsya kingdom the texts name no one. MBh 1.57; SB 9.22.6
Cedipa's line runs down to Damaghosha of Chedi, father of Shishupala. SB 9.22.6
Bhima of Vidarbha, Damayanti's father, stands in Vidarbha's line at an unrecorded remove. MBh 3.50
The third of Madhavi's four. MBh 5.114
Not a marriage: a drop of sweat in the sea, swallowed. Krittivasi Ramayana
Ahiravana's people found the child in the fish and brought him up. Krittivasi Ramayana
Their sixty thousand sons are counted, not named. SB 9.8.8
